title: 45-Day Identification Strategy
name: 45-Day Identification Strategy
metaDescription: 45-day identification strategy for Philadelphia 1031 exchange investors, building a defensible shortlist across Center City, Navy Yard, and University City submarkets.

sections.html: Forty-five days sounds like enough time until an investor is touring a Navy Yard warehouse on day 30 while still waiting on comparables for a Center City office assignment. In Philadelphia's competitive buyer pool, the identification window rewards investors who started building a shortlist before the relinquished property even closed, not after.

sections.heading: What The Clock Actually Measures
sections.html: The 45-day identification period starts on the day the relinquished property closes and runs on calendar days, including weekends and holidays, with no extension available for a slow appraisal or a distracted broker. The written identification has to name specific properties by legal description or address and go to the qualified intermediary before midnight on day 45. An investor who is still touring candidates on day 44 is not identifying; they are hoping, and hope is not a document the QI can file.

sections.heading: Starting The Search Before The Clock Starts
sections.html: The strongest Philadelphia identification lists get built during the marketing period for the relinquished property, not after closing. That means having a broker actively tracking Center City office listings, Navy Yard and I-95 corridor industrial inventory, and University City medical space near Penn, Drexel, or CHOP well before the sale closes, so the 45-day window is spent on diligence and negotiation instead of a cold search. Waiting until closing to start looking is the single most common reason an identification list ends up thin or rushed. An investor who begins that search only after the sale closes is essentially trying to compress weeks of broker relationship-building into the same window meant for final diligence and negotiation.

sections.heading: Building A List That Holds Up Under Either Rule
sections.html:
Most Philadelphia investors choose between the three-property rule and the 200% rule when structuring their list, and the choice should shape how candidates are gathered.

  • Confirm early whether the list will run under the three-property cap or the 200% valuation ceiling
  • Keep a standing shortlist of backup candidates in more than one submarket, since a single-market list concentrates risk
  • Verify that any rowhouse-to-multifamily conversion candidate has a realistic path to a use-and-occupancy certificate before its assigned closing date
  • Confirm recorded tax-abatement status on any candidate where the improvement value depends on it
  • Get written valuation support for every property that will appear on the notice, including the backup candidates and not only the leading choice

A list assembled this way survives contact with a lender's underwriting review far better than one built from a quick property search in the final week. It also gives an investor a real decision to make on day 40 instead of a forced one, since more than one candidate has already cleared a basic level of diligence.

sections.heading: Why Philadelphia's Buyer Pool Changes The Math
sections.html: A dense capital base drawn from New York, Washington, and regional investors means a well-located Philadelphia candidate rarely sits unsold for long, and a property that looked available on day 10 can be under contract to someone else by day 30. Identification strategy in this market has to account for that churn by naming more than one live candidate per asset class and keeping communication open with sellers even after a property is named on the list, since a named property is not a secured property until it closes. Keeping that relationship warm after identification, rather than assuming the deal is locked once the notice is filed, is part of protecting the exchange through the remaining months of the 180-day window.

sections.heading: What The Identification Notice Actually Requires In Writing
sections.html: The notice needs unambiguous legal descriptions or street addresses, must be signed by the investor, and must actually reach the qualified intermediary directly, rather than stopping at a broker or attorney's desk, before the deadline. Verbal mentions of a property to the QI do not count, and a fax or email sent after midnight on day 45 does not count either. Investors should confirm delivery in writing and keep a timestamped copy, since the burden of proving timely identification falls on the taxpayer if the exchange is ever reviewed. A confirmation email from the QI acknowledging receipt is worth keeping alongside the notice itself, since it closes the gap between when the document was sent and when it was actually received.

faqs.q: Does the 45-day clock pause for weekends or holidays in Philadelphia?
faqs.a: No. The 45-day identification period runs on consecutive calendar days from the closing of the relinquished property, with no extension for weekends, holidays, or delays outside the investor's control.

faqs.q: Can an investor change the identification list after day 45?
faqs.a: No. Once the deadline passes, the list is locked. Any property not named in writing before day 45 cannot be added later, even if a better candidate becomes available afterward.

faqs.q: Should a rowhouse conversion project be identified if it is still under construction?
faqs.a: It can be identified, but the investor should confirm a realistic path to a completed use-and-occupancy certificate before the exchange's closing deadline, since an incomplete conversion cannot close on schedule.

faqs.q: How many properties should a Philadelphia investor identify?
faqs.a: Enough to cover more than one submarket and asset class, given how quickly well-located candidates move in this buyer pool, while staying within whichever identification rule the investor has chosen.

faqs.q: Who is responsible for proving the identification was filed on time?
faqs.a: The taxpayer carries that burden. A timestamped, written notice delivered to the qualified intermediary before the deadline is the record that protects the exchange if it is ever questioned.
